name: Croissant
description: A crescent-shaped viennoiserie made from laminated yeast dough folded with layers of butter, giving a flaky crust and soft inside. The modern croissant was developed by French bakers in the early 20th century from the Austrian kipferl, introduced by a Viennese bakery in Paris.
how_to_eat: Eat it fresh in the morning, plain or dunked in coffee.
how_to_order: Ask for 'un croissant au beurre' (all-butter) at a boulangerie.

name: Jambon-beurre
description: A baguette sliced open, spread with butter and filled with slices of ham, also known as a 'parisien'. More than three million are sold in France each day, more than any other sandwich except the hamburger.
how_to_eat: Eat it on the go as a quick lunch.
how_to_order: Ask for 'un jambon-beurre' at a boulangerie or café counter.

name: Croque monsieur
description: A hot ham and cheese sandwich, traditionally made with Gruyère (sometimes Comté or Emmental), baked or fried; some brasseries add béchamel. It is mentioned as early as 1891, and with a poached or fried egg on top it becomes a croque madame.
how_to_eat: Eat it hot with a knife and fork, often with a green salad.
how_to_order: Ask for 'un croque-monsieur' (or 'croque-madame' with egg) at a café or brasserie.

name: Steak frites
description: A pan-fried beef steak (often entrecôte) served with French fries. It is a fixture of Paris brasseries and bistros.
how_to_eat: Eat with mustard or a sauce such as béarnaise or pepper sauce.
how_to_order: Order 'steak-frites' at a brasserie and say how you want it cooked: 'saignant' (rare) or 'à point' (medium).

name: Macaron
description: A sandwich confection of two almond-meringue shells (egg white, sugar and almond meal) joined by a filling such as ganache, buttercream or jam. The sandwich-style 'Paris macaron' is credited to Claude Gerbet or to Pierre Desfontaines of Ladurée, and comes in many colours and flavours.
how_to_eat: Eat at room temperature, a few at a time.
how_to_order: Buy by the piece or in a box at a Paris pâtisserie.

name: French onion soup
description: A soup of sautéed onions cooked in meat stock or water, topped with bread and cheese and browned under a grill. The modern gratinéed version dates from the mid-19th century around Les Halles, the old Paris food market.
how_to_eat: Eat it hot, breaking through the cheese crust with your spoon.
how_to_order: Ask for 'soupe à l'oignon gratinée' at a Paris brasserie.

name: Bouillabaisse
description: A Provençal fish stew from the port of Marseille, made with several kinds of local rockfish, olive oil, tomato, saffron and herbs. It is traditionally served with rouille sauce and toasted bread.
how_to_eat: Eat the broth first with bread and rouille, then the fish served on the side.
how_to_order: Order at a Marseille seafood restaurant, often a day ahead and for at least two people.

name: Ratatouille
description: A stewed vegetable dish from Nice made with tomatoes, aubergine, courgette, peppers, onion and garlic cooked in olive oil with herbs. It is served hot or cold as a side or main.
how_to_eat: Eat with bread, rice or alongside grilled meat or fish.
how_to_order: Ask for 'ratatouille niçoise' at Provençal restaurants.

name: Socca
description: A thin, crispy pancake made from chickpea flour, water and olive oil, baked in a very hot oven. It is a classic street snack of Nice.
how_to_eat: Eat hot with your fingers, sprinkled with black pepper.
how_to_order: Buy a portion from socca stalls in Nice's old town and markets.

name: Pissaladière
description: A flatbread from Nice topped with slow-cooked onions, anchovies and black olives. It is sold by the slice in bakeries across the Riviera.
how_to_eat: Eat a slice as a snack or light lunch.
how_to_order: Ask for a slice of 'pissaladière' at bakeries in Nice.

name: Salade niçoise
description: A salad from Nice of tomatoes, hard-boiled eggs, black olives and anchovies or tuna, dressed with olive oil. It is one of the best-known dishes of the Riviera.
how_to_eat: Eat as a main course in summer.
how_to_order: Order 'salade niçoise' at cafés in Nice and along the coast.

name: Pastis
description: An anise-flavoured spirit and apéritif, flavoured mainly with star anise and liquorice root, first commercialised by Paul Ricard in 1932. It turns cloudy when water is added and is especially associated with Marseille.
how_to_eat: Drink diluted with about five parts cold water, with ice.
how_to_order: Ask for 'un pastis' at any bar in Provence.

name: Calisson
description: An almond-shaped Provençal sweet of candied melon and orange peel ground with almonds, set on a thin wafer (pain azyme) and topped with royal icing. It has been a speciality of Aix-en-Provence since the 15th century and is one of the thirteen desserts of Provence.
how_to_order: Buy boxes from confectioners in Aix-en-Provence.

name: Quenelle
description: A soft, oval dumpling of creamed fish (traditionally pike) or meat with a light egg binding, sometimes with breadcrumbs, usually poached. Lyon and Nantua are famous for pike quenelles, often served with Nantua (crayfish) sauce and browned under a grill.
how_to_eat: Eat hot with a fork, straight from the baking dish.
how_to_order: Ask for 'quenelle de brochet sauce Nantua' at a Lyon bouchon.

name: Tartiflette
description: A baked dish from the Savoie Alps of potatoes, Reblochon cheese, lardons and onions. It is a popular hearty dish in ski resorts.
how_to_eat: Eat hot with a green salad and charcuterie.
how_to_order: Order at Alpine restaurants, especially in ski resorts in winter.

name: Fondue savoyarde
description: Melted cheese made from three local Savoie cheeses such as Beaufort, Abondance, Emmental de Savoie or Gruyère de Savoie, cooked with white wine and garlic in a communal pot. It is the French variant of Swiss cheese fondue; diners dip cubes of bread into it.
how_to_eat: Dip bread cubes on long forks into the shared pot, stirring as you go.
how_to_order: Order 'fondue savoyarde' for two or more at Alpine restaurants.

name: Raclette
description: Raclette cheese heated and scraped as it melts onto boiled potatoes, served with cornichons and pickled onions. The dish originated in Valais, Switzerland, but melted cheese was also traditionally eaten in Savoie and Haute-Savoie.
how_to_eat: Scrape the melted cheese over potatoes and eat with gherkins and charcuterie.
how_to_order: Order raclette for the table at Alpine restaurants in winter.

name: Gratin dauphinois
description: Thinly sliced raw potatoes baked slowly in cream in a buttered, garlic-rubbed dish, from the Dauphiné region of south-eastern France. Traditionally it contains no cheese.
how_to_eat: Eat as a side to roast or grilled meat.
how_to_order: Look for it as a side dish on menus in the Alps and Lyon.

name: Praline tart
description: A Lyon tart of crushed pink sugar-coated almonds (pralines roses) melted with cream in a butter shortcrust, giving a bright pink filling. It was created in the mid-1970s, via chef Alain Chapel, to give Lyon's bouchons a dessert.
how_to_order: Buy a slice of 'tarte aux pralines' at a Lyon pâtisserie.

name: Beef bourguignon
description: Beef braised slowly in red wine (often red Burgundy) and beef stock with carrots, onions, garlic and herbs, garnished with pearl onions and mushrooms. First documented in 1867, it became a standard of Paris bistros and only came to be seen as a Burgundian speciality in the 20th century.
how_to_eat: Eat with boiled potatoes, pasta or bread to soak up the sauce.
how_to_order: Order 'bœuf bourguignon' at bistros, especially in Burgundy.

name: Coq au vin
description: Chicken braised in red wine (traditionally Burgundy) with lardons, mushrooms and onions. It is a classic of Burgundy and French bistro menus.
how_to_eat: Eat with potatoes or bread for the sauce.
how_to_order: Order 'coq au vin' at traditional bistros.

name: Escargots de Bourgogne
description: Snails baked in their shells with garlic, parsley and butter, a famous starter from Burgundy. They are usually served by the half-dozen or dozen.
how_to_eat: Hold the shell with the tongs and pull the snail out with the small fork, then mop up the butter with bread.
how_to_order: Order 'une douzaine d'escargots' as a starter.

name: Gougère
description: A baked choux-pastry puff mixed with cheese, usually Gruyère or Comté. It is said to come from Burgundy, around Auxerre and Tonnerre in the Yonne, where it is served cold at wine tastings in cellars.
how_to_eat: Eat warm as an appetiser with a glass of wine.
how_to_order: Ask for gougères at bakeries and wine bars in Burgundy.

name: Oeufs en meurette
description: Poached eggs in meurette sauce, made with Burgundy red wine, bacon, onions and shallots browned in butter, served with toasted garlic bread. It is a traditional dish of Burgundian cuisine.
how_to_eat: Eat with the toast to soak up the sauce.
how_to_order: Order as a starter at Burgundian restaurants.

name: Kir
description: A cocktail of crème de cassis (blackcurrant liqueur) topped with white wine, traditionally Bourgogne Aligoté. It is named after Félix Kir, a former mayor of Dijon.
how_to_eat: Drink chilled as an apéritif.
how_to_order: Ask for 'un kir' at bars; 'kir royal' is made with Champagne.

name: Galette bretonne
description: A thin savoury pancake made from buckwheat flour, a speciality of Brittany. The classic 'complète' is filled with grated Emmental, ham and an egg.
how_to_eat: Eat folded with a knife and fork, with a bowl of cider.
how_to_order: Ask for 'une galette complète' at a crêperie.

name: Crêpe
description: A very thin pancake made from wheat flour, eggs and milk. Sweet crêpes are filled with sugar, jam, chocolate spread or fruit, and crêperies are found throughout France, especially in Brittany.
how_to_eat: Eat hot, folded, as a dessert or snack.
how_to_order: Ask for 'une crêpe beurre-sucre' or 'caramel au beurre salé' at a crêperie or street stand.

name: Kouign-amann
description: A round Breton cake made of bread dough layered with butter and sugar, which caramelise during baking. It originated in Douarnenez in Brittany around 1860.
how_to_eat: Eat warm, in small pieces, as it is very rich.
how_to_order: Buy by the slice or whole at Breton bakeries.

name: Moules marinières
description: Mussels cooked with white wine, shallots, parsley and butter, the best-known way of preparing mussels. They are usually served with fries as moules-frites, a dish from Belgium and northern France.
how_to_eat: Use an empty shell as tongs to pick out the mussels, then drink the broth.
how_to_order: Order 'moules marinières' (or 'moules-frites') at seaside restaurants.

name: Calvados
description: An apple (or pear) brandy from Normandy, distilled from cider and aged at least two years in oak casks. It is protected by an appellation d'origine contrôlée (AOC).
how_to_eat: Sip neat after a meal, or as a 'trou normand' between courses.
how_to_order: Ask for 'un calvados' at bars and restaurants in Normandy.

name: Tarte Tatin
description: An upside-down tart in which apples are caramelised in butter and sugar before the pastry goes on top and the tart is flipped. It is named after the Tatin sisters, who served it as the signature dish of their hotel in Lamotte-Beuvron in the 1880s.
how_to_eat: Eat warm, often with crème fraîche or ice cream.
how_to_order: Order as a dessert at bistros.

name: Choucroute garnie
description: Sauerkraut cooked with wine and juniper and topped with sausages, salted pork and potatoes. It is the signature dish of Alsace.
how_to_eat: Eat with mustard and a glass of Alsace white wine or beer.
how_to_order: Order 'choucroute garnie' at an Alsatian winstub or brasserie.

name: Tarte flambée
description: A very thin bread dough base topped with fromage blanc or crème fraîche, onions and lardons, baked in a wood-fired oven. It is a classic Alsatian dish meant for sharing.
how_to_eat: Cut into strips and eat with your hands, shared at the table.
how_to_order: Order 'une tarte flambée traditionnelle' at Alsatian restaurants.

name: Baeckeoffe
description: A casserole of potatoes, onions and three meats (typically pork, lamb and beef) marinated in Alsace white wine and slow-baked in a pot sealed with dough. Its name means 'baker's oven'.
how_to_eat: Eat straight from the earthenware pot with a green salad.
how_to_order: Look for it on winstub menus in Alsace.

name: Kougelhopf
description: A tall, ring-shaped brioche-style yeast cake with rum- or kirsch-soaked raisins and almonds, baked in a fluted mould. Long a celebration cake in Alsace, today it is mostly eaten at breakfast.
how_to_eat: Eat in slices for breakfast or with coffee.
how_to_order: Buy at Alsatian bakeries, often in small or large sizes.

name: Bretzel
description: A knot-shaped bread made with flour, water, butter and yeast, dipped in an alkaline solution before baking to give it a shiny brown crust, and sprinkled with coarse salt. It is a traditional symbol of Alsatian food and a common snack in bakeries and winstubs.
how_to_eat: Eat as a snack, often with beer.
how_to_order: Buy at Alsatian bakeries and Christmas markets.

name: Cassoulet
description: A slow-cooked casserole of white haricot beans with sausage, pork and often duck or goose confit, originating in Castelnaudary in Languedoc. Castelnaudary, Carcassonne and Toulouse each have their own version.
how_to_eat: Eat hot from the earthenware dish, breaking the crust.
how_to_order: Order at restaurants in Toulouse or Castelnaudary; portions are large.

name: Duck confit
description: Duck legs salted and slowly cooked in their own fat, then crisped before serving. It is a speciality of Gascony and the South-West.
how_to_eat: Eat with potatoes fried in duck fat ('pommes sarladaises').
how_to_order: Order 'confit de canard' at South-West restaurants.

name: Foie gras
description: The fattened liver of a duck or goose, served as a terrine or pan-seared. France is by far the largest producer, and most of its foie gras industry is in the South-West (Périgord, Aquitaine) and Alsace.
how_to_eat: Eat in thin slices on toasted bread, often with a sweet wine.
how_to_order: Order as a starter; 'mi-cuit' is lightly cooked, 'poêlé' is pan-seared.

name: Canelé
description: A small fluted pastry flavoured with rum and vanilla, with a dark caramelised crust and a soft custard centre. It is the signature pastry of Bordeaux.
how_to_order: Buy from pâtisseries in Bordeaux, often in boxes of several.

name: Piperade
description: A Basque and Gascon dish of onions, green peppers and tomatoes sautéed and seasoned with Espelette pepper. It is often served with eggs or ham.
how_to_eat: Eat as a side or with eggs or Bayonne ham.
how_to_order: Order in the French Basque Country around Bayonne and Biarritz.

name: Gâteau Basque
description: A round Basque cake of butter-rich shortcrust pastry (pâte sablée) filled with black cherry jam or almond or vanilla pastry cream. It is a traditional dessert of the French Basque Country, tied to the town of Cambo-les-Bains.
how_to_order: Buy at bakeries in the Basque Country; choose 'crème' or 'cerise'.
